transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-26 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Reyes (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Alex Cho (Redwood SE), Samantha Lee (Orchid Retail - Head of AI), Devon Martinez (Orchid - Platform), Priya Singh (Orchid - PM)
Shared links: demo deck https://redwood.ai/deck/hosted-demo, security whitepaper (placeholder link shared live)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we should be able to get through a hosted API demo in 30-ish minutes and then save five to ten for Q&A. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Samantha: Samantha here, thanks Jordan. Excited, we just want to see streaming and retry behavior mostly.
[00:13] Devon: Devon here. Platform questions — latency SLA and how retries interact with our gateway.
[00:18] Priya S: Priya from product, hi.
[00:21] Jordan: Awesome. Priya Nair from SE team will run the live demo. Priya, over to you.
[00:27] Priya N (SE): Cool thanks. So first slide, high-level — hosted API gives you text + chat endpoints, streaming support, and observability via Console. I'm gonna share the terminal and a quick SDK snippet.
[00:40] [screen share starts, small audio delay]
[00:45] Priya N: Right, here's a simple Node example: client.responses.create with model param, input as chat messages, and stream: true. Note that streaming returns chunks with delta tokens so you can render partial output fast.
[01:05] Samantha: Quick q — how do you handle token accounting for streaming? Does cost count full tokens or partial chunks?
[01:12] Priya N: Good question. Billing is per final token; streaming doesn't double-bill but you'll see token estimates in the response. Console also shows token breakdown per request. There might be minor estimation diffs but not double charging.
[01:27] Alex: Also we send final usage only once the response completes; interim streaming frames are for UX only.
[01:33] Devon: And if a client disconnects mid-stream?
[01:36] Priya N: If client disconnects, the server records tokens generated up until that point. You can configure shorter timeouts and keepalive on your side; we can also set an idle cutoff.
[01:45] Samantha: Ok makes sense.
[01:48] [01:48] Priya N: Next, params — temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences, and logit_bias if you need to nudge outputs. Example: temperature 0.2 for deterministic responses or 0.8 for more creative. We showed sample prompts for customer support summarization.
[02:10] [02:10] Jordan: We often recommend starting with temperature 0.0-0.3 for retrieval-augmented tasks where you want consistency.
[02:17] Samantha: When you say top_p alongside temperature do you recommend tuning both?
[02:20] Priya N: Typically tune one at a time; top_p can control nucleus sampling, so if you set temp low and top_p low you'll get very narrow outputs.
[02:28] Devon: Any automatic tuning suggestions in Console or Optimize?
[02:31] Priya N: Yes — Redwood Optimize analyzes your workload and suggests param adjustments and batching/quantization recommendations. We'll demo Optimize later.
[02:40] [02:40] Priya N (typing demo): Now I'm going to run a chat sample with streaming on.
[02:45] [02:45] Terminal shows stream frames arriving every ~120ms
[02:55] Priya N: See partial tokens arriving, we also surface a stable 'final' flag when completion is done.
[03:02] Samantha: Looks snappy. What about retries — if the request returns a 5xx, what's Redwood's recommended backoff?
[03:10] Alex: We recommend exponential backoff with jitter; default client SDKs have retry wrappers you can toggle. For idempotency make sure your calls are safe — attach a client-generated request_id and use the idempotency key header if replays are a concern.
[03:27] Devon: Is there an idempotency key supported out of the box?
[03:30] Alex: Yes, we support an Idempotency-Key header for create-like calls so retries won't double-run generation in the backend, but note that streaming partials may behave differently if you reconnect mid-stream.
[03:42] Samantha: Are retries counted against rate limits?
[03:45] Jordan: Retries count as requests; if you're getting transient 429s we suggest client-side retry with backoff and server-side rate-limit headers to respect. We also have token-level quotas and per-route throttling.
[03:58] Devon: On latency — what's the typical p95 for text generation for the models you host?
[04:03] Priya N: For our curated open models, p95 is model-dependent — for a mid-size chat model it's usually ~120-250ms per token on dedicated hardware; hosted varies by load but we publish performance profiles in the model catalog. We can share the benchmark sheet after.
[04:20] Samantha: Do you offer streaming for very long outputs? We sometimes generate multi-paragraph summaries.
[04:25] Priya N: Yes. Streaming is designed for long outputs; we also support partial flush thresholds so you can get deltas earlier. Also, KV cache is used for chat to avoid recomputing earlier tokens — although sometimes transcripts show this as K-V cash — we've seen the transcription do that.
[04:45] Samantha: ha yeah that happens.
[04:48] [04:48] Priya N: Moving to Console — I'll switch to the dashboard. You can filter by model, route, or API key, see per-request token breakdown, latency histograms, and error traces.
[05:05] [05:05] Screen shows Console logs, redwood-ui, slightly lagging due to screen share
[05:12] Priya N: Here is a route-level view; you can set rate-limits, per-route quotas, and enable automatic fallback to a cheaper model when latency spikes.
[05:24] Devon: Will fallback change output semantics? We care about consistency across rollouts.
[05:29] Priya N: Fallbacks will use compatible model variants — we recommend attaching model-version tags and testing behavior via eval sets. Console supports canary rollouts and A/B so you can measure regressions.
[05:40] Samantha: Is there a safety net for hallucinations or regression alerts?
[05:44] Jordan: Yes, Optimize integrates evaluation hooks: you can attach prompt sets, run continuous evals, and get regression alerts when quality drops below thresholds.
[05:54] Samantha: Great.
[05:56] [05:56] Priya N: Quick note on security — hosted API supports TLS, customer-provided keys, audit logs, and PII redaction options. For higher compliance we have Dedicated and Private deployment options with VPC and KMS/HSM integrations.
[06:12] Devon: For SOC 2 evidence, do you have a packaged bundle?
[06:16] Jordan: Yes we'll share the security whitepaper and SOC2 report link — we'll add that to the notes. (action)
[06:23] Samantha: Can we talk about costs — we need to compare to our current OpenAI spend.
[06:28] Jordan: Sure. For hosted we bill per token. There are levers to lower units: batching, prefix caching (for repeated context), and recommended quantized variants for cheaper throughput. Optimize can estimate cost impact for proposed configs.
[06:42] Priya N: Example: enabling prefix cache for chat reduces token generation by avoiding repeated system prompt sends; batching small requests can also greatly improve GPU amortization.
[06:55] Devon: Do you have a demo of batching?
[06:58] Alex: We can simulate — I'll run a small benchmark after this call. We'll also send the sample benchmark script.
[07:06] Samantha: Perfect.
[07:09] [07:09] Priya N: Back to streaming/retries - implementation notes: SDKs support stream:true, and the HTTP API supports SSE for streaming as well. For retries, we recommend idempotency-key + exponential backoff with randomized jitter. Remember to log request_id so you can correlate in Console.
[07:30] Devon: For our gateway we want deterministic retry behavior so we'll add idempotency keys. Any gotchas?
[07:35] Alex: Only thing is if your app expects exactly-once side effects triggered by a model output, you need to make side effects idempotent on your side. Model outputs are not transactional.
[07:47] Samantha: Understood.
[07:50] [07:50] Priya N: Now, small demo of Optimize — here's a workload profile and suggestions: lower temperature for routing rules, enable batching for the customer-support route, and a recommendation to use a quantized model variant for nighttime batch generation. It shows estimated cost delta.
[08:12] Samantha: How accurate are those cost deltas?
[08:15] Priya N: They're estimates based on token distributions and throughput; real-world results can vary but we've found them directionally accurate. We'll provide a bench spreadsheet.
[08:24] Devon: Any constraints for using quantized models with streaming? Does it affect latency?
[08:28] Priya N: Quantized models can have slightly higher per-token latency for some ops, but often much better throughput/cost tradeoff. The runtime chooses kernels that work best given the hardware.
[08:40] Samantha: Switching gears — can you do a short walkthrough of a real request from our app to Redwood?
[08:45] Priya N: Sure. We'll mock a support summarization flow. Sending messages array with user/system messages, model x-redwood-chat-1, stream true, temperature .2, max_tokens 512.
[09:02] [09:02] partial tokens stream in on screen
[09:10] Priya N: There's also a retry header example here. If you see a 429 include Retry-After header respecting server guidance.
[09:19] Devon: If we see persistent 5xx under load what should we do?
[09:23] Jordan: Open a support ticket and we can analyze traces; for mission-critical workloads we recommend Dedicated capacity so you have reserved GPU pools and predictable throughput.
[09:35] Samantha: What's the threshold to trigger Dedicated conversation usually?
[09:39] Jordan: It's usage and latency requirements — often mid-to-large customers above a commit threshold or who need strict data isolation. We'll work with your finance & infra teams on that.
[09:50] Devon: For the hosted SLA do you provide SLOs for latency?
[09:55] Priya N: Hosted has best-effort latencies published per model; Dedicated comes with SLA-backed latency and uptime targets.
[10:03] [10:03] Priya N: Quick note — console also surfaces per-token cost so you can attribute spend to routes and teams. That helps with chargebacks internally.
[10:15] Samantha: That will help our finance folks.
[10:18] [10:18] Priya N: Any more product questions?
[10:21] Samantha: One last on data retention — how long do logs live by default?
[10:25] Jordan: Default retention is 30 days for request logs on hosted, configurable for enterprise accounts. We can arrange longer retention in Dedicated with auditing.
[10:34] Devon: For privacy we need to ensure PII redaction — do you support automated redaction?
[10:38] Alex: We have PII detection/redaction toggles; you can also configure custom redaction pipelines before logs are stored.
[10:45] Samantha: Great.
[10:48] [10:48] Jordan: Ok, quick recap and next steps: we'll send pricing & security docs, Priya will share the benchmark script and sample prompts, and we'll schedule a POC scoping call. Any timeline constraints?
[11:01] Samantha: We'd like to kick a POC in early October if possible.
[11:05] Jordan: Sounds good — we'll aim for week of 10/6.
[11:09] Devon: I'll loop in infra and confirm a VPN/peering contact.
[11:13] Jordan: Perfect.
[11:15] [11:15] Priya N: That's all from us, thanks everyone.
[11:18] Samantha: Thanks all.
